Manasā
(‘created by मिन्द्’)
------------------------------------------
Manasā is the goddess controlling all the reptiles, especially the snakes. Her worship is very common in Bengal and Assam.
The story goes that when the people of the world, unable to bear the affliction created by snakes, approached the great sage Kaśyapa—whose offsprings were these snakes—for succour, he created the goddess मनसा by using his mental powers (manas = मिन्द्) as the presiding deity and controller of the reptiles.
She pleased शिव and विष्णु through her severe austerities and obtained several boons from them.
Jaratkāru was her another name.
She was married to a sage whose name also was जरत्कारु and gave birth to a son, आस्तिक by name. He later on succeeded in stopping the सर्पयाग or serpent-sacrifice of the king जनमेजय, the son of परीक्षित्.
She is known by many other names such as Trijagadgaurī, Śivā, वैष्णवी, Nāgamātā, Viṣaharā, Mṛtasañjīvanī, Siddhayoginī and so on. Repetition of her twelve names is said to give full protection against poisonous reptiles.
Her images show her as a goddess with two arms, one holding a snake and the other in abhayamudrā. She may also be shown with four arms and a seven-hooded snake as a parasol, along with her husband (the sage जरत्कारु) and her child आस्तिक.

mantradraṣṭā
(‘seer of a [Vedic] मन्त्र’)
------------------------------------------
Vedas, the basic scriptures of हिन्दुइस्म्, are considered as ‘apauruṣeya’ (not man-made), but as revelations of God Himself through certain ṛṣis or sages. These sages only ‘saw’ (dṛś = to see) these mantras and uttered them. Hence they came to be known as mantradṛk or मन्त्रद्रष्टा.
Vasiṣṭha, वामदेव, Madhucchandā, मेधातिथि, दीर्घतमस्, Asita देवल and विश्वामित्र are some of these sages.
There are at least 27 women sages also.
Before reciting a Vedic मन्त्र, three things have to be stated. The first is the ṛṣi or the sage to whom it was revealed. The second is the छन्दस् or the metre. The third is the devatā or the deity to whom it is addressed.

Manmatha
(‘one who churns the मिन्द्’)
------------------------------------------
Also known by other names such as Madana (one who intoxicates) and Kandarpa (one who was arrogant towards ब्रह्मा the creator), he was born out of ब्रह्मा himself as the personification of bewitching (male) physical beauty. He got the boon that he could entice anyone with lust. When he tried this power on ब्रह्मा himself, creating uncontrollable lust in him towards सन्ध्या, his own daughter, he cursed मन्मथ to be reduced to ashes by शिव.
When this happened, he was restored to life again, by शिव himself who was moved by the piteous wailings of रति (Manmatha’s wife) as also the interventions of the gods.
His distinguishing features are the bow of sugarcane stalk, a bunch of five kinds of flowers as arrows, fish as his flag-symbol and the मकर (mythical crocodile) as his carrier. रति is his consort.
Actually मन्मथ and रति are the archetypes of physically perfect man and woman. मन्मथ is akin to Eros or Cupid.

mānasa-snāna
(‘mental bath’)
------------------------------------------
Before the performance of any ritua-listic act, taking स्नान or a bath is compulsory. However, sometimes, due to some valid reasons like illness, decrepitude (due to old-age) or non-availability of facilities to take bath, it is not possible to fulfil this requirement. Under such circumstances, the धर्मशास्त्रस् have provided some alternatives like मन्त्र-स्नान and मानस-स्नान.
In मन्त्रस्नान one has to sprinkle a little water on the head with the repetition of the मन्त्र ‘āpo hi ṣṭhā mayo bhuvaḥ....’ (Ṛgveda 10.9.1-3).
In मानस-स्नान, one has simply to repeat in the मिन्द् any name of Lord विष्णु and feel that he has been purified by that divine name.
See also SNĀNA.

manomayakośa
(‘the sheath of the मिन्द्’)
------------------------------------------
The मनस् or मिन्द्, along with the pañcajñānendriyas or the five organs of knowledge, form the ‘manomayakośa’ or the sheath of मिन्द्. Like a sheath, it covers and hides the real nature of the आत्मन् or the Self. It is a part of the sūkṣma-śarīra (also called लिङ्ग-śarīra), the subtle body, the other two parts being प्राणमयकोश (sheath of vital airs) and vijñānamayakośa (sheath of intellect).
See PAÑCAKOŚAS.

mantrasaṁskāra
(‘refining of the मन्त्र’)
------------------------------------------
The तन्त्रस् are a highly specialised literature dealing exclusively and exhaustively with the mantras of the various deities of the Hindu pantheon. Before these mantras are used for any purpose—sacred or secular—they have to be purified ceremonially. This is called ‘mantra-saṁskāra’.
Mantrasaṁskāra comprises ten rituals. They are: जनन (extraction of the letters of the मन्त्र through a specially drawn drawing called मातृकायन्त्र); जीवन (writing the letters of the मन्त्र got from the process of जनन, in the prescribed order and doing जप of each letter preceded by Oṁ, to infill it with life); ताडन (striking each letter with sandal-water, repeating ‘yaṁ’); बोधन (beating the letters of the मन्त्र with red oleander flowers [Nesium odorum] to the accompaniment of the syllable ‘raṁ’); अभिषेक (bathing the same letters of the मन्त्र [written on a metal plate as prescribed] with water using an अश्वत्थ leaf [Ficus religiosa] and the syllable ‘raṁ’); vimalīkaraṇa (purifying the मन्त्र with the special formula ‘oṁ hraum’ while contemplating on it); āpyāyana (satiating the letters of the मन्त्र in water in which कुश grass or a flower is immersed, using the same मन्त्र [oṁ hraum] which is called ‘jyotirmantra’); तर्पण (offering libations of water to the मन्त्र to the accompaniment of the same jyotirmantra); दीपन (illuminating the मन्त्र with the formula ‘oṁ ह्रीṁ śrīm’); gupti (keeping the मन्त्र as a great secret thus protecting its power).
All these are highly esoteric in nature and should be done under the expert guidance of a competent गुरु.

Manusmṛti
(‘the स्मृति of मनु’)
------------------------------------------
The Manusmṛti—among the Hindu religious works—has the unique distinction of being thoroughly misunderstood and even reviled, in the modern days, especially in post-independence India. However, it goes to the credit of मनु himself (4.176) that rules which cause widespread resentment among the people, even if they are धर्म (by earlier standards), should be given up. This is akin to changing the constitution if the people of a country so desire.
The extant Manusmṛti which compri-ses 12 adhyāyas or chapters, has 2694 ślokas or verses in the anuṣṭubh metre.
Scholars have battled for years to establish the identity and the time of मनु, the author of this treatise. He is certainly not one of the 14 मनुस् (progenitors of mankind and rulers over the manvantaras) mentioned in the epics and the पुराणस्. He must have been a great sage and an erudite law-giver since he has been widely quoted by many a writer of धर्मशास्त्रस्.
The present work probably took the final shape during the period 200 B. C.—A.

. Though it contains earlier and later strata, as seen from quite a few conflicting or contradictory statements on the same point, the number of recasts do not seem to be many.
Sometimes, a theory is hazarded that the extant Manusmṛti is a work based on an earlier one called Mānavadharmasūtra. This, however, has been rejected by well-known scholars in this field (vide Dr. P. V. Kane, History of Dharmaśāstra, vol. 1, part 1, p. 149, Poona, Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, 1968).
A brief account of the contents of the extant work may now be given:
Chapter 1 (119 verses)
Creation of the world and various creatures; divisions of time; varṇadharmas or duties of the four castes; greatness of the ब्राह्मण.
Chapter 2 (249 verses)
On धर्म; divisions of the land of भारतवर्ष as Brahmāvarta, आर्यावर्त and so on; saṁskāra; definitions of the terms आचार्य, उपाध्याय and others.
Chapter 3 (286 verses)
Eight forms of मर्रिअगे; mutual relation between husband and wife; pañca-yajñas or five daily sacrifices; śrāddha and तर्पण (obsequial rites).
Chapter 4 (260 verses)
Means of livelihood; rules of conduct; condemnation of immoral enjoyments; efficacy of आचार or good conduct.
Chapter 5 (169 verses)
Causes of death; on ड़ोओद् and drink; अशौच or ceremonial impurity; duties of women.
Chapter 6 (97 verses)
Exhaustive treatment of the Vāna-prasthāśrama.
Chapter 7 (226 verses)
Political science and statecraft including the details like punishment for transgressions, taxation, appointment of ministers, espionage, envoys and political expedients.
Chapter 8 (420 verses)
Administration of justice; eighteen titles of law such as ṛṇādāna (non-repayment of debt), asvāmivikraya (sale of property by one who is not the legal owner), vetanādāna (non-payment of wages), sīmāvivāda (boundary dispute), vibhāga (partition) and so on.
Chapter 9 (336 verses)
Duties of men and women; इन्हेरितन्चे; succession; strīdhāna (property of women); and, gains of learning.
Chapter 10 (131 verses)
Duties of ब्राह्मणस्; mixed castes; आपद्-धर्म (duties in emergencies).
Chapter 11 (265 verses)
Duties of a स्नातक (a brahmacāri who has completed his studies); sins and their expiation.
Chapter 12 (126 verses)
Results of good and bad deeds; nature and knowledge of the आत्मन्, the Self within; benefits of studying the Manusmṛti.
The Manusmṛti has several Sanskrit commentaries. The bhāṣyas of मेधातिथि (A.
), Govindarāja (Manvāśayānu-sāriṇī) (A.
) and the Manvartha-muktāvalī of Kullūka (earlier than A.

) are more well-known among them. नारायण (Manvarthavivṛti), Rāghavā-नन्द (Manvarthacandrikā), नन्दन (Nandinī) and Rāmachandra are the other commentators about whom not much is known.
The Manusmṛti seems to have influenced the law-books of some other countries outside India also. The Culovaṁśa of Ceylon (now Sri Lanka), the Kutasa Mānava and the Dawagama of Indonesia have been greatly influenced by मनु.
Works very similar to Manusmṛti have been found in China and Japan. A deity of the old Persian pantheon has been called ‘Vaivasvata मनु’. Darius (600 B. C.) is said to have framed his laws according to मनु’s work. There is a statue of मनु in the Philippines.
In later works, two more treatises—the Bṛhanmanu and the Vṛddhamanu—have been referred to. It is difficult to say whether they were independent works or redactions of Manusmṛti.
See also MANVANTARA.

Manonmanī
(‘one who makes our मिन्द् eager [to attain her]’)
------------------------------------------
She is one of the aspects of the Divine मोथेर् पार्वती dear to सदाशिव, more common in South India. She is worshipped for bhūti (prosperity) and also for striking fear in the minds of enemies.
Iconographical works describe her in various ways. The most common description is that she is of the colour of the मोओन् with a benevolent appearance. She has four arms, holding a red and a blue lotus in two hands, the other two being in varada and abhaya mudrās. Sometimes, a rosary is shown instead of the blue lotus.
Other works show her with five faces and ten arms carrying śūla (spear), टङ्क (hammer), पाश (noose), aṅkuśa (goad), घण्टा (bell), fire and lotuses.
She may also be shown as surrounded by 46 Śaktis and an equal number of Kanyās (virgin-deities).

Māndhātṛ
------------------------------------------
Māndhātṛ was a great king. He was the son of the king Yavanāśva. He got this name because as the new born baby he was sustained by drinking nectar oozing out of इन्द्र’s thumb. (Indra is said to have remarked, ‘mām dhāsyati,’ ‘He will suck my thumb’).
His wife was Bindumati. पुरुकुत्स, अम्बरीष and मुचुकुन्द (all of whom proved to be great kings and devotees of God) were his sons.
He successfully performed one hundred अश्वमेध and राजसूय sacrifices.
He is said to have fought Lavaṇāsura and was killed by him.

Mantrayoga
(‘yoga through मन्त्र’)
------------------------------------------
The Vāyavīya Saṁhitā is an important work on शैविस्म्. It describes योग as of five kinds. मन्त्रयोग is the first in the series. It is that योग in which, by the constant repetition of the मन्त्र imparted by the गुरु, the mental states become steady.
When this is associated with prāṇā-yāma or breath-control, it is called Sparśa-योग. स्पर्शयोग develops into भावयोग when mantrajapa or the repetition of the मन्त्र stops automatically, leaving only the भाव or feeling. By further practice, the world appearance in its various forms, disappears, thus leading to Abhāvayoga.
At the last stage of spiritual evolution union with शिव is attained. This is महायोग.
The eight steps of योग described in the Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) are also included in this practice.

Mantra Rahasya
------------------------------------------
This is a tāntrik work dealing exclusively with mantras of various types used in black-magical rites. It is in five paricchedas or sections along with a परिशिष्ट or appendix which is also fairly long.
The whole work is in the form of ślokas in the anuṣṭubh metre.
Only a brief synopsis may be attempted here:
First Pariccheda
It deals with the षट्कर्मस् exhaustively, in all their aspects. The षट्कर्मस् (six types esoteric rites) are: śāntikaraṇa (offsetting the evil effects of diseases or evil planetary effects); vaśīkaraṇa (bringing a person under one’s control); stambhana (arresting the movement of any person or living being); vidveṣaṇa (creating enmity between friends or relatives); उच्चाटन (forcing a person to leave the place); māraṇa (bringing about the death of someone disliked).
Before undertaking the actual performance of these karmas the following factors have to be reckoned with: suitable time (as determined by referring to the almanac); dik or direction; modes of meditation on the related deities; some preliminary information about the mantras in general; āsanas or postures to be adopted; shape and size of the kuṇḍas (pits for the fire); rules concerning the establishment of kalaśas (ceremonially established pots of water).
Some details about जप (repetition of the मन्त्र) like the method of counting by fingers or the rosary as also the nyāsas are also described.
The method of performing हवन or होम (fire-ritual) along with associated details is also given.
Second Pariccheda
The षट्कर्मस् are explained in detail along with the mantras to be used.
By the śāntikaraṇa rites the effects of diseases like fever and of sorcery rites done by others can be remedied. Great details for the latter rite are given as also the particular मन्त्र to be used. By wearing a prescribed यन्त्र (mystical diagram drawn on a base like a metal plate) on the body many results can be obtained. For instance: offsetting the evil effects created by anyone; a barren woman conceiving; children being freed from the menace of evil spirits and so on.
By the vaśīkaraṇa rites one can bring under control any person like a woman, the king, the boss, or anyone else at will.
By performing the stambhana rites one can arrest the movements of any person or any weapon, the power of speech of an enemy, the power of fire to burn, stop the army of the enemy or his ship and so on.
Next comes vidveṣaṇa. By performing this rite one can bring about intense mutual hatred between persons so far well-disposed towards each other.
After this comes mohana (deluding a person), by which anyone seen by the sādhaka becomes deluded and does his bidding. This is an additional rite.
The उच्चाटन procedure and मन्त्र enable the sādhaka to drive away or displace his enemy.
The book adds one more rite here called ‘ākarṣaṇa’, meant to attract anybody towards oneself.
Last comes māraṇa. This ritualistic action is aimed at getting an enemy of धर्म or society killed. This has to be followed by the recitation of Kavacamantra to protect oneself.
The text has given several mantras as also related religious rites to achieve these results, in great detail.
Third Pariccheda
Bhūtinīs are a certain class of spirit-goddesses. They are nine. The firstpart of this chapter deals with the sādhanās connected with their worship. Different modes of their worship along with the mantras are stated as also the results of their vision.
For instance, the sādhaka, by pleasing Bhūtinī, can get plenty of ड़ोओद्, clothing and ornaments as also wealth.
If the sādhaka pleases Naṭī, she can become his servant-maid and do his bidding.
Similarly कामेश्वरी makes him a king and Kumārikā bestows कुबेर’s wealth.
Then the text mentions the names of eight Nāginīs (another class of female deities) and the results of their worship.
This is followed by शवसाधना (repeating the given मन्त्र, sitting on a dead body, at dead of night on the new मोओन् day) and its result.
Then, the names of six Kinnarīs (another class of goddesses) and the sādhanās connected with them are described.
Next comes the description of certain mantras and yantras (mystical diagram) by which one can get protection against the dangers created by evil persons, thieves, animals like the elephant or lion.
The science of reviving a dead person (mṛtasañjīvinī-विद्या) is given at the end.
Fourth Pariccheda
The following are the topics dealt with in this chapter: various medicines that can cure a person bitten by a poisonous serpent; special medicines that can help a barren woman to conceive; some yantras inscribed on bhūrja-patra (the bark of birch) meant to be worn on the arm by a barren woman to get children; शवसाधना (practising जप seated on a dead-body); method of doing पुरश्चरण using a dead-body.
Fifth Pariccheda
Sādhanās connected with the pleasing of the female deities—Aṣṭanāyikās—like Jayā, Vijayā, and Svarṇamālā including their mantras are given first.
Mantras and yantras that help one to control the spirits like डाकिनी are described next.
Method of knowing one’s date and time of death, mantras that help one to protect himself from poisonous beings, mantras that help cure children possessed by evil spirits and help pregnant women to have a smooth delivery are also given.
Pariśiṣṭa
This is an appendix given at the end. It deals with Vśīkaraṇa of various kinds and many miscellaneous topics.

manvādi-tithi
(‘the day on which a मन्वन्तर starts’)
------------------------------------------
There are fourteen manvantaras. (See MANVANTARA for details.) Each of these manvantaras is said to begin on a particular day. This is called ‘manvādi-tithi’.
The following are the fourteen manvādi-tithis:
Āśvina-śukla-navamī (9th day of the bright half of Āśvina); Kārttika-śukla-द्वादशी (12th day of the bright half of Kārttika); चैत्र-śukla-tṛtīyā (3rd day of the bright half of चैत्र); Bhādrapada-śukla-tṛtīyā (3rd day of the bright half of Bhādrapada); अमावास्या of Phālguna (new-मोओन् day of Phālguna); Pauṣa-śukla-एकादशी (11th day of bright half of Pauṣa or पुष्य); आषाढ-śukla-daśamī (10th day of the bright half of आषाढ); Māgha-śukla-saptamī (7th day of the bright fortnight of Māgha); Śrāvaṇa-कृष्ण-aṣṭamī (8th day of the dark half of Śrāvaṇa); pūrṇimā (full-मोओन्) of the months of आषाढ, Kārttika, Phālguṇa, चैत्र and Jyeṣṭha.
These manvādi-tithis are considered extremely good for the performance of śrāddhas to appease the पितृस् or the manes.

Mantrārthābhidhāna
------------------------------------------
See MĀTṚKĀNIGHAṆṬU.

mānasa-pratyakṣa
(‘direct perception by the मिन्द्’)
------------------------------------------
Perception of objects in order to get a knowledge about them is an important topic discussed in the Indian philosophical systems. Normally, the मिन्द् gets the direct knowledge of an object through the five organs of knowledge or ज्ञानेन्द्रियस्. However, sometimes, a knowledge can arise in the मिन्द् directly also. For instance, when we see a rose from a distance, the मिन्द् can also comprehend its smell, from previous experiences. This is called ‘mānasa-प्रत्यक्ष’.
According to the Kumārila’s (A.

) school of Mīmāṁsā philosophy, a person gets the knowledge of himself as the सोउल् or Self, different from the body, directly in his मिन्द् as the “I”—consciousness. This is termed in that school as ‘mānasa-प्रत्यक्ष’.
See also YOGIPRATYAKṢA.

manvantara
(‘period of rule or epoch of a मनु’)
------------------------------------------
The concept of time as given in the पुराणस् is, to say the least, मिन्द्-boggling!
Each day of ब्रह्मा, the creator, (called ‘kalpa’ by the पुराणस्) includes one thousand Mahāyugas. Each Mahāyuga includes the four well-known युगस्: कृतयुग, त्रेतायुग, द्वापरयुग and कलियुग.
This day or कल्प is divided into fourteen manvantaras (epochs of मनु) or periods of time, ruled by a मनु. Each मन्वन्तर has a little more than 71 Mahāyugas.
The fourteen मनुस् ruling over these manvantaras of the present कल्प are: Svāyambhuva, Svārociṣa, Uttama, Tāmasa, Raivata, Cākṣuṣa, वैवस्वत, Sāvarṇi, दक्ष-sāvarṇi, Brahma-sāvarṇi, धर्म-sāvarṇi, रुद्र-sāvarṇi, Ruci and Bhauma.
The मनु of the present age is वैवस्वत. He is the son of सूर्य and is also known as Śrāddhadeva.
Each मनु has his own set of gods, इन्द्र, ṛṣis and others. The name of the present इन्द्र is Purandara. The सप्तर्षिस् or the Seven Sages of this मन्वन्तर are: वसिष्ठ, कश्यप, अत्रि, जमदग्नि, गौतम, विश्वामित्र and भरद्वाज.
In terms of human years, one Mahāyuga is of the duration of 43,20,000 years. Hence the period of a मन्वन्तर comes to 308 million human years!

manas
(‘that by which one thinks’)
------------------------------------------
It is an aspect of the अन्तःकरण or internal organ, responsible of सङ्कल्प or general thinking, including willing and विकल्प or doubting. It is an evolute of the combined सत्त्व-aspect of all the five तन्मात्रस् or primordial elements.
See also MIND.

mantrasnāna
(‘bathing through मन्त्र’)
------------------------------------------
See MĀNASA-SNĀNA and SNĀNA.

Mantrālaya
------------------------------------------
Originally a small village called Mañcāle, and now a well-known place of पिल्ग्रिमगे, मन्त्रालय is famous for its बृन्दावन (See BṚNDĀVANA) of the great sage and mystic राघवेन्द्रतीर्थ (A.

-1671). He is said to have entered into it while still alive. (See RĀGHAVENDRA-TĪRTHA.). It is situated on the bank of the river Tuṅgabhadrā, in the Kurnool district of Andhra Pradesh at a distance of 93 kms. (58 miles) from the railway junction of Guntakal.
मन्त्रालय Temple">A view of मन्त्रालय TempleApart from this बृन्दावन, there are three more, of other saints.
An image of god वायु (wind-god) as also a shrine for Mañcālāmbikā (an aspect of पार्वती) are the other attractions for the devotees.
There is a heavy rush of pilgrims throughout the year. Desires of the devotees who serve the sage in the prescribed manner are fulfilled.
मन्त्रालय">Bṛndāvana at MantrālayaAccording to the local legends, this was the place where प्रह्लाद, the great devotee of Lord विष्णु had worshipped the goddess Mañcālāmbikā and had also performed वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्.
The place is now well-developed with good arrangements for the benefit of the devotees and pilgrims.

Mantrapuṣpa
------------------------------------------
This is a short piece forming a part of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka (1.22.1 to 7). It is primarily used in the worship of सूर्य (the Sun-god) as also in सूर्य-नमस्कार. It is also used to offer flowers at the end of ritualistic worship.
The sun, the मोओन् and the स्तर्स् (sūrya, चन्द्र and नक्षत्र) appear to rise from the waters of the ocean for an onlooker. Hence they have been called puṣpa or flowers of the water. One who knows them as such reaps great benefits like having children and cows.

Mantrayoga Saṁhitā
------------------------------------------
This is a fairly exhaustive work dealing with all aspects of मन्त्र, दीक्षा (initiation), पूजा (worship), mudrās (poses of hand and fingers), nyāsas (purification of limbs), जप, जपमाला (rosary) and other related topics.
A brief synopsis of the contents is as follows:
Mantrayoga (meditation on ब्रह्मन् through names, forms and bījākṣaras); need for दीक्षा or initiation; need for a गुरु and his characteristics like knowledge of all śāstras (sciences), self-control, expertise in ritualistic actions and truthfulness; characteristics of शिष्य or disciple like desirelessness, obedience, self-control and devotion to the deity; some preliminary details regarding दीक्षा like referring to certain चक्रस् or diagrams like Nāmacakra, Rāśicakra, Nakṣatracakra and Akaḍamacakra which help in deciding about the मन्त्र to be given; deciding the right time for दीक्षा by referring to the पञ्चाङ्ग (almanac) as for month or week or day; details regarding the proper place and the right मन्त्र; the five deities for upāsanā (meditation) which are शिव, देवी, विष्णु, गणेश and सूर्य; the five deities as related to the पञ्चभूतस् (five elements); three kinds of भक्ति or devotion; various kinds of śuddhis or purification like sthānaśuddhi (purification of the place of meditation); different kinds of āsanas or seats like those of wool, deer-skin and tiger-skin; ten kinds of सṁस्कारस् (purification) for a मन्त्र; प्राणायाम; हवन or होम; पूजा with several उपचारस् (modes of service) like daśopacāra; three kinds of जप; different bījamantras for different deities; some bījas like hrīm, klīm, krīm and aim; method of keeping the count of the मन्त्र by hand; different kinds of japamālās (rosaries) made of रुद्राक्ष beads (Elaeocarpus ganitrus), seeds of lotus plant, gems and so on; meditation on the different forms of deities with details; several forms of विष्णु (7 forms), देवी (24 forms), शिव (5 forms), गणपति (2 forms) and सूर्य (2 forms); description of समाधि; मिन्द् and its various aspects.
There is no doubt that this treatise is an extremely useful handbook of sādhanā.

Mānasāra
------------------------------------------
Architecture, town planning, building construction, इचोनोग्रफ्य् and allied topics were well-known to the Hindus right from the most ancient times. The epics and the पुराणस् contain innumerable references to the same.
One of the most standard works containing a well-organised body of this knowledge (called शिल्पशास्त्र) is the Mānasāra of an unknown author.
As available now, the book has 70 chapters and 10,000 lines in Sanskrit. It goes into great detail about all aspects of architecture, townplanning and icono-graphy, including casting of images in metals. Sixteen types of village and town plans are described.
The original work might have been composed during the Gupta period (A.
-525). The extant (redacted version) work probably belongs to 11th to 15th centuries.

manana
(‘reflecting in the मिन्द्’)
------------------------------------------
This is the second of the three direct disciplines prescribed for getting the knowledge of the आत्मन् and its oneness with ब्रह्मन्. It is defined as constant thinking of ब्रह्मन्, already heard from the spiritual preceptor, strengthening it by लोगिच् which is in consonance with the purport of Vedānta.

Mandara
------------------------------------------
When the देवस् (gods) and दानवस् (demons) wanted to churn the ocean of milk, kṣīrasāgara, to get अमृत or ambrosia, they are said to have used the मन्दर (or Mandāra) mountain as the churning rod. विष्णु supported the mountain on his back, in his इन्चर्नतिओन् as कूर्म or the tortoise.
Mandara mountain is sometimes enumerated among the seven ‘Kula-parvatas,’ mountains that act like the borders of the islands of this earth.
A hill situated about 50 kms. (30 miles) south of Bhagalpur in Bihar has been identified with the मन्दर of the पुराणस्.

Mānasa-sarovara
(‘lake [that emerged out of ब्रह्मा’s] मिन्द् or heart’)
------------------------------------------
One of the most sacred places of पिल्ग्रिमगे for a Hindu is the mount कैलास and the lake मानस-सरोवर. The four-faced ब्रह्मा while doing penance in the हिमालयस् is said to have created it out of his मिन्द् (or heart). Hence the name.
मानस-सरोवर">A view of Mānasa-sarovaraIt is in Tibet, at a distance of 32 kms. (20 miles) from the mount कैलास. Several rivers like the Sindhū (Indus), Sutlej and ब्रह्मपुत्र originate from here. Its water is crystal clear and very cold. It is 90 metres (300 ft.) deep. It abounds in swans and ducks. There are eight maṭhas or monasteries on its banks, some of them containing the images of Hindu gods like Kālī.
It is situated at a height of 4500 metres (15,000 ft.) above the sea-level.
A bath in it is considered highly meritorious. Its actual circumference is 89 kms. (55 miles). However, the route of circumambulation is 113 kms. (70 miles).
Those who visit this lake, often undertake the circumambulation of the mount कैलास also which takes about 2 to 3 days.
There is a twin lake called Rākṣasa-tāl, where रावण is said to have performed तपस् (austerity) to please Lord शिव.

mantra
(‘that which protects when reflected upon’)
------------------------------------------
One of the most widely used words in Sanskrit religious literature is the word ‘mantra.’ It is, etymologically speaking, defined as that which protects (tra = to protect) when repeated and reflected upon (man = to think, to reflect).
This word has two meanings: the poetical part of the वेदस् and, the names and syllables used to indicate or propitiate deities. The former is Vedic and the latter is tāntrik.
The वेदस् are generally divided into two broad divisions: the मन्त्र and the ब्राह्मण. The मन्त्र part of the first three वेदस् is again classified as ṛk, yajus and सामन्. The ब्राह्मणस् are in prose, deal with the details of sacrificial rites and quote the appropriate mantras (sacred formulae) to be used in the rites.
In the मन्त्र section, a fourth category, the निगद, is sometimes added. Nigadas are, strictly speaking, not mantras but instructions uttered loudly by one priest to another, during a sacrificial rite.
There are several rules in the Śrauta sūtras (See ŚRAUTASŪTRAS.) about the recitation of the Vedic mantras.
The most famous of all the Vedic mantras which is popular and very much in vogue even today is the गायत्री-मन्त्र.
The latter kind of mantras appear in the earlier पुराणस्. They extol the greatness of the पञ्चाक्षरी or ṣaḍākṣarī (mantra of five or six letters namaśśivāya and oṁ namaśśivāya), अष्टाक्षरी (of eight letters—oṁ namo nārāyaṇāya) and dvādaśākṣari (of twelve letters—oṁ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya) mantras and a few others.
However it is the तन्त्रस् or Śāktā-gamas that developed the art and science of the mantras, both extensively and intensively. Various types of mantras for the various deities of the Hindu pantheon along with different bījākṣaras (See BĪJAMANTRA.) and their usages have been dealt with in the well-known works like the Prapañcasāra, Śāradātilaka and Mahānirvāṇatantra.
For more details see under TANTRAS.

Mānasollāsa
(‘that which exhilarates the मिन्द्’)
------------------------------------------
There are two well-known works of this name.
The first is an exhaustive gloss (vārttika) by सुरेश्वर (A.
) on the famous hymn Śrī दक्षिणामूर्ति Stotra of शङ्कर (A.

-820). The total number of ślokas or verses on the ten verses of the original is 367. It discusses all aspects of Advaita Vedānta and also tries to refute other schools like न्याय, Vaiśeṣika, Sāṅkhya and Śaiva. There is also a detailed exposition of the mahāvākya (the great sentence or Vedic dictum) tat tvam asi.
This Mānasollāsa has a Sanskrit commentary, Mānasollāsa Vṛttānta, by one रामतीर्थ (17th century A. D.). This commentary explains the original hymn also.
The second one is a voluminous work on the dharmaśāstra and allied branches, by the Cālukyan king Someśvara III who ruled from A.
to A.

. This work is also called Abhilaṣitārtha-Cintāmaṇi. It has five books, each containing 20 chapters. It deals with 100 different topics connected with the royal household and the royal court.
Some of the subjects dealt with in this work are: general and religious एथिच्स्; social service; मर्रिअगे and rearing of children; making of इदोल्स्; private and inter-state law; architecture; painting; अस्त्रोलोग्य्; alchemy; मुसिच् and musical instruments.
The original author himself has given his own commentary called Dharma-pradīpikā.

mānuṣa-liṅga
(‘śivaliṅga made by human beings’)
------------------------------------------
Lord शिव is worshipped in the form of a लिङ्ग, an emblem with a rounded surface, cylindrical in shape. Liṅgas are classified into several varieties, of which the मानुष-लिङ्ग is also one. It is defined as a लिङ्ग prepared by the mānavas or human beings and worshipped by them.
The iconographical works give all the details needed to prepare such a लिङ्ग. The ritualistic processes for installing the लिङ्ग in a temple are given by the शैवागमस्, religious texts dealing with the worship of Lord शिव.
See ŚIVALIṄGA for more details.

mantrasiddhi
(‘the potency of the मन्त्र being fully roused’)
------------------------------------------
Though a मन्त्र received from a qualified गुरु in the traditional manner has its potency, this has to be fully roused to make it effective in the practical field.
One of the methods is पुरश्चरण (See PURAŚCARAṆA for details.).
Sometimes, this process of puraś-चरण may have to be repeated two times more.
If the power is not roused even after this, then the sādhaka or the spiritual aspirant, under the direct guidance of the गुरु, has to take to the sevenfold procedure starting with bhrāmaṇa and ending with dāhana (vide Mantrayogasaṁhitā 67).
This procedure has to be directly learnt and practised under the guidance of an adept in the field.
A simple method suggested by some of the पुराणस् is ‘akṣara-lakṣa-जप’. It is the same as repeating the मन्त्र as many lakhs of times as there are letters in the मन्त्र. For instance, to get मन्त्रसिद्धि in the six-lettered मन्त्र, ‘Oṁ namaś-śivāya,’ one has to repeat it 6 lakh times.

Mantramahodadhi
------------------------------------------
The Mantramahodadhi, as its very name indicates (‘A Great Ocean of Mantras’), is a work of encyclopaedic nature, dealing exhaustively with the mantras treated in the various tāntrik treatises. It was composed by महीधर who has written a commentary on the Mādhyandinaśākhā of the Śuklayajurveda saṁhitā.
Mahīdhara lived in the 16th century. At the end of this work he mentions that he completed it on the śukla-aṣṭamī day of the month of Jyeṣṭha (May-June) in the Vikrama-saṁvatsara 1645 (i.e. A.

).
He belonged to the Vatsa-गोत्र and was the son of Phanūbhaṭṭa, a great devotee of राम. He was born at Ahicchatra located in the Bareilly district of Uttar Pradesh.
Being disgusted with the worldly life he came to काशी and settled there, spending his time in worshipping and meditating on god नरसिṁह. He wrote this treatise at the request of his son Kalyāṇa as also some learned ब्राह्मणस्.
The work has 25 Taraṅgas and contains 3300 verses, all in the anuṣṭubh metre. The author himself has written a lucid commentary also, named as Naukā.
A brief synopsis of the contents may now be attempted here:
First Taraṅga (206 verses)
Preliminary details connected with mantrajapa, worship of deities and some special mantras along with the nyāsas like Ṛṣyādinyāsa are given here.
The commentary explains some bījamantras or seed-letters such as yaṁ, vaṁ and raṁ as also the selection of the site for पुरश्चरण (See PURAŚCARAṆA for details.).
Second Taraṅga (135 verses)
This section deals extensively with the various mantras of गणेश or गणपति.
Some of the different aspects of गणपति described here are उच्छिष्ट-गणपति; शक्ति-गणपति; लक्ष्मी-विनायक; Trailokyamohana-गणेश; हरिद्रा-गणपति.
Various mantras of these aspects are also given.
Elaborate kāmya prayogas (rites for the fulfilment of desires) (for e.g., removal of poverty) are described.
Third Taraṅga (75 verses)
A short section, this deals with the mantras of Kālī that bestow fluency of speech immediately. A special यन्त्र (mystical diagram) is also described.
Some rites of वामाचार (See under TANTRAS.) have also been mentioned.
Fourth Taraṅga (124 verses)
The rites of the goddess तारा and her yantra—the Tārādhāraṇayantra—are described here. Many fruits of her worship such as poetical ability, longevity and honour by a king are also mentioned.
Fifth Taraṅga (95 verses)
The mantras of the following goddesses are dealt with here: तारा एकजटा, Nīlasarasvatī and Vidyārājñī.
The pūjāyantra of Nīlasarasvatī containing 64 lotus petals and 64 Śaktis in them is also described.
Sixth Taraṅga (99 verses)
The mantras of the goddesses छिन्नमस्ता, रेणुका, शबरी, मधुमती, Svyaṁvarakalā, Pramadā and others have been given here.
Four yantras, of which that of Svayaṁvarakalā deserves special mention.
Seventh Taraṅga (112 verses)
Mantras of some more goddesses like Vaṭayakṣiṇī, Viśālayakṣiṇī, शीतला Vārtālī and Mātaṅgī are described here.
Worship of Vārtālī can be used to destroy enemies since she is known as Śatrughātinī (destroyer of enemies).
Eighth Taraṅga (144 verses)
This taraṅga opens with the famous Bālāmantra (of three syllables of the goddess Bālā-त्रिपुरसुन्दरी.
The various ingredients needed to prepare the tilaka (forehead mark) as also some information about the 64 योगिनीस् are the other topics discussed.
Ninth Taraṅga (132 verses)
The goddesses dealt with here are: अन्नपूर्णा, गौरी, Jyeṣṭālaṣmī and others. Worship of the fierce goddess Pratyaṅgirā for destroying one’s enemies is also described.
Tenth Taraṅga (120 verses)
Mantras of the deities Bagalāmukhī, Svapnavārāhī and others along with four yantras are described here.
Eleventh Taraṅga (111 verses)
This taraṅga gives a detailed explanation of the worship of Śrīvidyā (the मन्त्र of Lalitāparameśvarī or ललिता-त्रिपुरसुन्दरी, consisting of 15 letters [Pañcadaśākṣarī] or 16 letters [Ṣoḍa-śākṣarī]. The method of drawing the श्रीचक्र or Śrīyantra and its worship is also mentioned.
Twelfth Taraṅga (172 verses)
The fifteen परिवारदेवतास् (goddesses forming the retinue) like कामेश्वरी, Bhagamālinī, Tvaritā and Vicitrā are described along with their mantras. The Bagalāmantra is the longest with 136 syllables.
Thirteenth Taraṅga (122 verses)
This section deals with the worship of हनुमान्. The main मन्त्र has 12 syllables. The mālāmantra has more than 500 syllables. Four yantras, of which the Hanumad-dhāraṇa-यन्त्र is extremely important, are also given.
Fourteenth Taraṅga (130 verses)
Mantras of विष्णु, including those of Lakṣmīnarasiṁha, are described here.
Fifteenth Taraṅga (109 verses)
This deals with the mantras of Ravi (Sun), मङ्गल (Mars), गुरु (Jupiter) and शुक्र (Venus). Their usages in fulfilling one’s desires are also given.
Sixteenth Taraṅga (136 verses)
This taraṅga gives the following mantras along with their kāmyaprayogas (methods or rites prompted by desires):
Mahāmṛtyuñjayamantra (50 syllables); mantras of रुद्र, कुबेर, गङ्गा and the goddess Maṇikarṇikā.
Rudrapūjana-यन्त्र is also given. Its worship gives all-round prosperity.
Seventeenth Taraṅga (117 verses)
Kārtavīryārjuna has been considered as an इन्चर्नतिओन् of the सुदर्शनचक्र of विष्णु. His mantras are given here.
Establishing a lamp on a यन्त्र of कार्तवीर्यार्जुन and worshipping it for the fulfilment of desires is also described.
Eighteenth Taraṅga (212 verses)
The longest of all, this taraṅga describes the method of reciting the Caṇḍī as also the rite of शतचण्डी.
A few black-magical rites like Mohana (deluding others), उच्चाटन (driving away one’s enemies) and Māraṇa (destruction of one’s enemies) are given towards the end.
Nineteenth Taraṅga (149 verses)
This section contains the mantras of Śāstā—called Caraṇāyudha-śastṛ—as also those of सदाशिव, Pinākin, महादेव and Hara (all being names of शिव).
Twentieth Taraṅga (131 verses)
This deals with various kinds of yantras or mystical diagrams and their use in fulfilling one’s desires. More than 25 yantras have been described. Some of them are: Dhanikavaśyakara; Rāja- mohana; Duṣṭamohana; Vijayaprada; Pativaśyakara; Māraṇa.
Twenty-first Taraṅga (170 verses)
Some rituals to be done daily are described here such as daily worship, bath (by invoking the river goddesses), wearing the tilaka or religious mark on the forehead, recitation of Gāyatrīmantra and so on.
Twenty-second Taraṅga (179 verses)
This contains detailed analyses as also explanations of many holy rites like mudrās, arghyas, puṣpāñjalis etc., which are associated with worship.
Twenty-third Taraṅga (100 verses)
Offering of the damana flowers (a kind of jasmine, Jasminum multiforum) and the पवित्र (prepared out of thread) to various deities is described here. Mantras of Kāmadeva and रति as also Kāmagāyatrī are also given.
Twenty-fourth Taraṅga (131 verses)
This taraṅga describes the various चक्रस् (or diagrams) like the Akaḍamacakra, the Akathahacakra, Rāśicakra and Nakṣatracakra by which a मन्त्र suitable for a sādhaka can be selected.
Ten methods of saṁskāra or refinement of mantras like दीपन (kindling), बोधन (awakening) and ताडन (striking) are described at the end.
Twenty-fifth Taraṅga (132 verses)
This last chapter is specially devoted to the षट्कर्मस् of Vāmācāratantra (See ṢAṬKARMAS for details.).
On the whole this is an encyclopaedia work on mantras, covering all the important aspects.
However, one word of caution has to be uttered here. As a rule, any मन्त्र has to be received ceremonially (through दीक्षा) from a competent teacher before practising it.
As regards the black magical rites given at the end, they are to be used only against the enemies of the society and hardened criminals and that too through proper channels.
Even the desire-motivated rituals should be resorted to sparingly, as a last resort.
When sincere prayer to God can give us everything we need, why depend on other means?
